result: Goal set: read the delivered documents in order and answer detailed questions on the retellings, ignoring unrelated documents. This will now anchor every prompt in this session.
OK

Vira Toland (born 1912, Ostrey Hollow) recounts the 1919 "water in the cans" scandal at the Ansel Keddie milk-testing station, revealing years later that Keddie was actually skimming cream, which fractured the Keddie and Brant families despite their marriage ties.
This report is from 1966 (recommending a levy for 1967, not 1908) and contains no mention of a year 1908 levy at all.

Effie Loomis (Association secretary 1901–1940) writes an institutional history noting Article VII made each skimming station's own test final and unappealable, then documents the 1925 arbitration that paid Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 while "finding no cause established," and flags an unexamined 1923 crate of condemned measuring equipment never mentioned at the hearing.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie's own statement and unsent letter (spring 1925) describe in detail his rigorous, unchanged testing procedure and point to an unexplained anomaly—tests jumping to 3.80 for nine weeks in 1911 while using a borrowed measure—insisting he never skimmed cream despite being dismissed.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ivy Keddie, Ansel Keddie's granddaughter, presents to the Ordell County Historical Society (1959) the scientific vindication: the station's pipettes were mechanically short by 5%, exonerating her grandfather and proving no cream was ever stolen—just a defective measuring instrument that skewed tests low for 26 years.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper (1905–1945), explains the "station gain" ledger line he invented—a steady 5¼% surplus between credited and actual cream fat from Ostrey Hollow—and argues Keddie's single-handed control of the station made pilferage structurally possible, while noting manager Selby Vose knew of the gain and told him to drop it.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn, retired state dairy inspector, compiles his year-by-year circuit notes on Ostrey Hollow (1907–1936), documenting always-true scales and no added water, and crucially his 1923 discovery that the station's pipettes were condemned for failing to deliver their calibrated mark—later replaced with glass that tested true.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym, curator, compiles catalogue accession notes for 16 physical items in the Ordell County dairy collection—invoices, ledgers, test books, the pipette crate, inspection reports, and bulletins—documenting the paper trail behind the Ostrey Hollow cream-testing controversy and its 1958 scientific resolution.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Selby Vose, the Association's manager, delivers his 1926 annual address defending the 1919 water-in-the-cans circular and the $3,800 settlement, insisting the real cause was patrons watering their milk (which stopped once scrutiny began) and dismissing the condemned testing apparatus as mere routine wear-and-tear housekeeping, not a cause.
The error code returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days is `SKF-2201`.

Roy Brant, Emmet Brant's son at Hessel Bottom, presents his father's 1898–1929 weigh book showing the scales always agreed with the station's while the tests still ran 0.17 points low year-round, and recounts the family rift with brother-in-law Ansel Keddie after the 1919 water circular.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage for Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

Rosalie Cudd, cheesemaker at Alder Corners (Vessey County), writes to Ivy Keddie in 1958 supplying her father's independent 1915–1930 test records for the four Hessel Bottom farmers who hauled to his factory in summer—consistently around 3.78–3.82—corroborating that their milk was never watered or thin regardless of what Ordell County believed.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Leland Vaught, dairy husbandry professor, writes the introduction/method section of Bulletin No. 471 (Oct. 1958) explaining how an under-delivering pipette produces a proportional, self-consistent, internally undetectable low test, and presents the Ostrey Hollow measurements and the 1911 borrowed-measure episode as proof the station's glass—not watered milk or bad hay—caused the shortfall.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

Dell Rundle, schoolteacher at Larrow Green, writes the Association's 1939 fiftieth-anniversary jubilee pamphlet recounting its founding, Article VII, and the Ostrey Hollow "cream theft" quarrel as settled valley opinion—then adds a 1959 footnote about Ivy Keddie's college reinvestigation and a same-year "note added while in press" where he retracts his own stolen-cream narrative after seeing the ledger's "station gain" entry showing cream arrived heavy, not light.
Message No. 219, filed by Perley Dunmore, was 6 words.

Alonzo Frick, the attorney who chaired the 1925 board of arbitration, recalls in this 1946 bar association piece hearing three competing explanations (watered milk, a skimming tester, bad hay) for Ostrey Hollow's low tests, believing Keddie's denial yet noting Keddie privately admitted he'd always suspected the patrons themselves, and reflects that the board paid out $3,800 without ever identifying a true cause.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, the Association's buttermaker at Larrow Green for 41 years, recalls that Ostrey Hollow's cream always weighed in heavier than the office's paperwork claimed, insists the Hollow's true test was about 3.85 and that "somebody was helping the cans along," and recounts lending his own glassware to open the station in May 1896 before its own outfit arrived.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the "Trebbin norm."

Nyle Grigg, chairman of the 1908 investigating committee, republishes his original report in 1919 with a cover letter claiming his committee sampled Hessel Bottom "through the whole of 1908" and that Bulletin No. 214 confirmed bog hay depresses tests by "two tenths"—both claims conflicting with the reprinted report itself (which says sampling covered only January–March) and with other documents' citation of that same bulletin's much smaller findings.
The level-27 accessor removed at API level 31 is `chart.rawCells()`.

Dr. Roland Kepp, a veterinary surgeon, argues before the Farm Club in 1926 that Hessel Bottom's sour, mineral-poor soil—not the testing station—explains the milk's chronic 0.21-point fat deficit, citing Bulletin No. 214 (misstated as showing a "two tenths" depression) and dismissing the 1911 six-week anomaly as meaningless summer noise.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.

Hazel Brant, Roy Brant's daughter and final keeper of the family weigh book, recalls in a 1981 oral-history tape the same 1910 leaf (3.42 test), the 0.19-point year-round shortfall, the Keddie family ties, and Ivy's 1958 discovery of the pipette crate in the loft — but introduces new/conflicting details: Orra as Emmet's *half* sister "by his father's second wife" (contradicting r09's insistence she was a *full* sister), glassware condemned in "twenty-one" (1921, differing from other 1923 dates), and the arbitration hearing placed in "twenty-six" (1926, not 1925).
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta (the woman called Tuesday's scarf).

Duncan Keddie, Ansel and Orra's son and Ivy's father, writes 1968 family notes (with a 1970 addendum) setting out genealogy and the provenance/whereabouts of the five key books and the crate — while asserting Orra was Emmet's *full, younger* sister (conflicting with r17's "half sister") and dating the glassware's condemnation to 1923, its discovery by Ivy to February 1958, and confirming three arbitration sessions (two held at the station itself, matching r13).
The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers died by accidental drowning from a fall off the unrailed flume edge while working, with no evidence of another person's involvement.

Narrator: *The Ashlin Chronicle*, front-page news feature (3 Oct. 1958) announcing Bulletin No. 471's exoneration of Ansel Keddie, dramatizing Ivy's ladder-climb discovery of the crate and the pipette measurements — while introducing fresh discrepancies of its own, calling Ivy Ansel's "great-niece" (not granddaughter, per r18) and Rosalie Cudd "Jerome Cudd's niece" (not daughter, per r10), and citing eleven pipettes measured.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon, historian of Ammon & Sons (dairy glass supplier at Tarnet), writes a 1949 company-history chapter reproducing the firm's own 1897 invoice ($77.93, six dozen 17.6cc pipettes) and its evasive 1923 reply letter, offering the glassblower's theory that a reground mold caused a consistently short-pouring lot to pass undetected.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle.

Cleve Oram, the cream hauler's son who rode the Ostrey Hollow wagon route as a boy, recalls the station's physical layout and loft, the 1925 hearing (which he pegs at $3,500 and 67,000 lb), his father's lifelong belief that cream was skimmed off rather than a glassware fault, and Ivy's 1958 discovery — while introducing new discrepancies (5 dozen measures purchased, Ivy called Hazel's "first cousin once removed" rather than second cousin, and a claimed Keddie-Vose cousin tie that Duncan's notes explicitly deny).
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Orin Falke, the Ordell County agricultural agent, compiles a 1959 official summary report for the county board tracing the whole Ostrey Hollow affair to Bulletin No. 471's pipette conclusion — then appends a note retracting his own concession to the wet-hay theory after finally reading Bulletin No. 214's actual (much smaller) figures, and correcting his own report's error that called Ivy Keddie "great-niece" rather than granddaughter.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, retired clerk at the Cooperative's Larrow Green office for 25 years, writes a 1953 historical-society memoir on the paperwork side of the affair — confirming the "station gain" ledger line, the four exhibits carried to arbitration, and Selby Vose's parentage — while introducing new date conflicts: the pipette condemnation placed in "twenty-two" (1922) rather than 1923, the arbitration award dated "twenty-four" (1924) rather than 1925, and the 1896 partial-season intake given as "eleven hundred thousand pounds" (yet another figure, contradicting both r14's "nine hundred thousand" and the catalogue's claim that no such figure survives).
The color named in the third paragraph is teal (the endpapers of the collected edition with Halvane's diagram).

Orra Keddie's own diary (1897–1930, published 1964 with editorial notes) records the household year-by-year — the 1919 circular delivery, the resulting rift with her brother Emmet, the 1925 dismissal, and Ansel's quiet later years — while stating the circular went to "eleven families" (versus "nine" in r09 and r17) and giving her own birth year as 1866 (versus 1868 in Duncan's notes).
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.

Wrote three files — `answers-part1.md` (Section A, stories 1–4), `answers-part2.md` (Section A, stories 5–8, and Section B), `answers-part3.md` (Sections C–G) — answering all 31 numbered questions (A's 8 stories, B1–B4, C1–C5, D1–D3, E1, F1, G1).
